title: 1 Kings 2:36–46
context: The king sends for Shimei and says, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, and live there, and don’t go anywhere else” On the day he goes out and passes over the brook Kidron, he will surely die, and his blood will be on his own head. Shimei answers, “What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do.” He lives in Jerusalem many days. At the end of three years, two of his slaves run away to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath. Shimei is told, saddles his donkey, goes to Gath, and brings the slaves back. Solomon hears that he had gone from Jerusalem to Gath and had come again, and he summons him. He reminds Shimei that he had adjured him by the LORD and warned him, “Know for certain that on the day you go out and walk anywhere else, you shall surely die”, and that Shimei had said, “The saying that I have heard is good.” He asks why Shimei has not kept the oath of the LORD and the commandment instructed to him. He adds that Shimei knows in his heart all the wickedness he did to David, and that the LORD will return that wickedness on his own head, while King Solomon will be blessed and David’s throne will be established before the LORD forever. The king commands Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; he goes out and falls on Shimei, “so that he died.” The chapter closes, “The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.” Both traditions describe the confinement, the broken condition, and the execution as the narrator reports them, without sensationalizing the death or turning the settlement into a party debate about succession. Evaluations of the severity of the terms, like those of David’s charge in verses 8–9, may differ within both traditions.

verses.text: The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, and live there, and don’t go anywhere else.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Build yourself a house in Jerusalem, and live there, and don’t go anywhere else”. The speech continues into the next verse. Confinement to Jerusalem, in a house he is to build, is the first term Solomon sets.

Arminian readers hear a real restriction offered as a way to live. Shimei is not immediately put to death; he is told to settle in the city and not to go anywhere else.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also take the command as a present alternative to death. A house in Jerusalem, life there, and a ban on going elsewhere are the terms named.

Both traditions describe the order as the narrator gives it, and they wait for the penalty attached in the following verse.

verses.text: For on the day you go out and pass over the brook Kidron, know for certain that you will surely die. Your blood will be on your own head.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“For on the day you go out and pass over the brook Kidron, know for certain that you will surely die. Your blood will be on your own head.” The boundary is the brook Kidron, and the penalty is death, with the blood placed on Shimei’s own head if he crosses it.

Arminian readers hear a condition plainly stated. The day he goes out and passes over Kidron is the day he will surely die, and he is told that in advance.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same certainty: “know for certain that you will surely die.” and “Your blood will be on your own head.” The brook is the line named.

Both traditions take the terms as public and clear. Kidron is the bound the king sets; the verse does not require a full map of the valley.

verses.text: Shimei said to the king, “What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do.” Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days.
verses.arminianNotes:
Shimei said to the king, “What you say is good. As my lord the king has said, so will your servant do.” Shimei lived in Jerusalem many days. He accepts the saying as good and promises to do it, and he remains in the city for a long time.

Arminian readers hear a free consent. Shimei himself calls the king’s word good and pledges to keep it, and for many days he does live in Jerusalem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the acceptance in view, because later Solomon will quote a form of it back to him. “What you say is good.” is Shimei’s present word.

Both traditions mark the interval: the agreement is made, and many days pass in Jerusalem before the next event.

verses.text: At the end of three years, two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath. They told Shimei, saying, “Behold, your slaves are in Gath.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“At the end of three years, two of Shimei’s slaves ran away to Achish, son of Maacah, king of Gath.” They told Shimei, “Behold, your slaves are in Gath.” The peace of the many days is broken by a flight to a Philistine court already known from David’s story.

Arminian readers take the three years and the news as a real interval and a real temptation. The slaves are in Gath, and Shimei is told where they are.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note the dated notice. Three years end, the slaves run to Achish son of Maacah, king of Gath, and Shimei hears of it.

Both traditions describe the report as the occasion of what follows, without deciding for Shimei, in this verse, what he will do.

verses.text: Shimei arose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his slaves; and Shimei went and brought his slaves from Gath.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Shimei arose, saddled his donkey, and went to Gath to Achish to seek his slaves; and Shimei went and brought his slaves from Gath.” He does not send; he goes, and he succeeds in bringing them back.

Arminian readers hear a chosen journey. The condition had named going out; Shimei arises, saddles the donkey, and goes to Gath and back for his slaves.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the double wording: he went to Gath to seek them, and he went and brought them from Gath. The trip is not left in doubt.

Both traditions report the journey as the narrator gives it. Recovery of the slaves is the aim he acts on; the terms of verses 36–37 remain in place.

verses.text: Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and had come again.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon was told that Shimei had gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and had come again.” The king hears not only of the going out but of the return.

Arminian readers take the report as the means by which the broken term comes to light. Shimei has already come again; the journey is finished when Solomon is told.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note both movements in the report: gone from Jerusalem to Gath, and come again.

Both traditions let this brief notice stand between the journey and the hearing. The king will now speak.

verses.text: The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Didn’t I adjure you by the LORD and warn you, saying, ‘Know for certain that on the day you go out and walk anywhere else, you shall surely die’? You said to me, ‘The saying that I have heard is good.’
verses.arminianNotes:
The king sent and called for Shimei, and said to him, “Didn’t I adjure you by the LORD and warn you, saying, ‘Know for certain that on the day you go out and walk anywhere else, you shall surely die’? You said to me, ‘The saying that I have heard is good.’” Solomon recites the oath of the LORD, the warning, and Shimei’s own acceptance.

Arminian readers hear him held to words he had received and approved. The adjuration was by the LORD, and Shimei’s “The saying that I have heard is good.” is now brought back to him.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also note a small difference of wording: the original warning had named passing over the brook Kidron, while this recital speaks of going out and walking “anywhere else”. The substance is the same prohibition, and the verse should not be pressed into a contradiction.

Both traditions take the hearing as a recalling of a sworn term, not as a new law invented on the spot.

verses.text: Why then have you not kept the oath of the LORD and the commandment that I have instructed you with?”
verses.arminianNotes:
“Why then have you not kept the oath of the LORD and the commandment that I have instructed you with?” The question names two things broken: the oath of the LORD, and the king’s commandment.

Arminian readers hear a real charge of unfaithfulness. Shimei had sworn, in effect, by accepting an oath of the LORD, and he has not kept it.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the double wording: oath of the LORD, and commandment instructed by the king. The broken term is not treated as a private slip only.

Both traditions leave the question as Solomon’s indictment, and they turn with him to the older wickedness he will now name.

verses.text: The king said moreover to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the wickedness that you did to David my father. Therefore the LORD will return your wickedness on your own head.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king said moreover to Shimei, “You know in your heart all the wickedness that you did to David my father. Therefore the LORD will return your wickedness on your own head.” The present breach is joined to the older curse against David, and the return of that wickedness is ascribed to the LORD.

Arminian readers hear both the inner knowledge and the moral claim. Shimei knows in his heart what he did to David, and Solomon says the LORD will return it on his own head.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise keep the therefore. The journey to Gath is not isolated from the grievous curse David had named; the LORD will return that wickedness on Shimei’s own head.

Both traditions report this as Solomon’s verdict in the LORD’s name, without using it to invent a party dispute about succession ethics.

verses.text: But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be established before the LORD forever.”
verses.arminianNotes:
“But King Solomon will be blessed, and David’s throne will be established before the LORD forever.” The contrast is blessing and an established throne, set over against the returned wickedness of the previous verse.

Arminian readers hear a confession about the throne, not only a sentence on a man. David’s throne is to be established before the LORD forever, the hope already heard in the charge and in the word about David’s house.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers stress the same pairing: Solomon blessed, and David’s throne established before the LORD forever.

Both traditions take the line as the king’s claim for the house of David under the LORD, shared ground with the earlier prayer for peace on that throne, not a cue for a new fork here.

verses.text: So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he went out, and fell on him, so that he died. The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
verses.arminianNotes:
“So the king commanded Benaiah the son of Jehoiada; and he went out, and fell on him, so that he died. The kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.” The execution is told in the same spare wording used earlier, and the chapter ends with the kingdom established in Solomon’s hand.

Arminian readers let both sentences stand. Shimei dies as Benaiah falls on him, and the narrator then states that the kingdom was established in Solomon’s hand, a close already foreshadowed when Solomon first sat on David’s throne.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers hold the same restraint about the death: “he went out, and fell on him, so that he died.” The final clause is the book’s own summary of the unit and of the chapter.

Both traditions report the execution as the narrator gives it, without sensationalizing it, and they receive the last sentence as the narrative close: the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon.
